scenes.visual: Title card 'Landis's Blocked Capillary' over a single capillary drawn in cross-section. Reuses the first film's COLOUR MAP: hydrostatic push ORANGE arrows; oncotic pull BLUE arrows; red cells RED; lymph GREEN; walls charcoal. Numbers appear only as on-screen text.

scenes.tts: Capillary walls let water and small solutes through. So why doesn't all your plasma end up in your tissues? Something must hold most of it in.
scenes.visual: A capillary with a dotted, leaky charcoal wall; small water droplets seep out between wall cells into the surrounding tissue. A plasma 'level' gauge on the side starts to drop, then a question card freezes it.
scenes.narration: Capillary walls let water and small solutes through. So why doesn't all your plasma end up in your tissues? Something must hold most of it in.

scenes.tts: The first film showed that blood flows down a pressure difference, divided by a resistance. Across the capillary wall, the same rule decides which way fluid moves.
scenes.visual: Brief replay of the first film's pinned rule 'Q = (P_in − P_out) / R' and its ORANGE pressure line. The tube rotates so the 'in' and 'out' sides become the inside and outside of the capillary wall.
scenes.narration: The first film showed that blood flows down a pressure difference, divided by a resistance. Across the capillary wall, the same rule decides which way fluid moves.

scenes.tts: Two pressures act across the wall. The first is blood pressure inside the capillary, minus the tissue fluid's pressure outside. It pushes fluid outward. Physiologists call it hydrostatic pressure.
scenes.visual: ORANGE arrows press outward from inside the capillary through the wall, labelled 'push: hydrostatic pressure, P_c − P_i'. A smaller ORANGE arrow from the tissue side presses back, labelled 'P_i'.
scenes.narration: Two pressures act across the wall. The first is blood pressure inside the capillary, minus the tissue fluid's pressure outside. It pushes fluid outward. Physiologists call it hydrostatic pressure.

scenes.tts: The second comes from plasma proteins, mostly albumin. Few cross the wall, so they pull water back in. Protein outside pulls the other way, so the difference counts. That pull is the oncotic pressure.
scenes.visual: Round blocks labelled 'albumin' sit inside the capillary, held back by a fuzzy coat lining the wall; one or two slip through, label 'few cross'. A few blocks sit in the tissue outside. BLUE arrows point inward from the tissue toward the plasma, labelled 'pull: oncotic pressure, π_c − π outside'. ORANGE and BLUE arrows now face each other across the wall.
scenes.narration: The second comes from plasma proteins, mostly albumin. Few cross the wall, so they pull water back in. Protein outside pulls the other way, so the difference counts. That pull is the oncotic pressure.

scenes.tts: In eighteen ninety-six, Ernest Starling, working with dogs, argued that these two pressures set the direction of flow. But neither had been measured inside a single capillary.
scenes.caption: In 1896, Ernest Starling, working with dogs, argued that these two pressures set the direction of flow. But neither had been measured inside a single capillary.
scenes.visual: Caption 'Ernest Starling, 1896'. A balance scale appears with an ORANGE weight 'push' on one pan and a BLUE weight 'pull' on the other. Over a single capillary, a gauge reads '?'.
scenes.narration: In 1896, Ernest Starling, working with dogs, argued that these two pressures set the direction of flow. But neither had been measured inside a single capillary.

scenes.tts: In nineteen twenty-seven, Eugene Landis took up the test in frogs. He spread out the mesentery, the thin sheet that holds the gut, and watched single capillaries under a microscope.
scenes.caption: In 1927, Eugene Landis took up the test in frogs. He spread out the mesentery, the thin sheet that holds the gut, and watched single capillaries under a microscope.
scenes.visual: Caption 'Eugene Landis, 1927'. A cartoon frog outline; a thin, nearly transparent sheet unfolds beside a loop of gut, with a fine network of capillaries. A microscope circle zooms in on one capillary. Label 'schematic'.
scenes.narration: In 1927, Eugene Landis took up the test in frogs. He spread out the mesentery, the thin sheet that holds the gut, and watched single capillaries under a microscope.

scenes.tts: A fine glass pipette slid into one capillary to record its pressure. Then he pressed the capillary shut with a fine glass rod.
scenes.visual: A thin glass pipette enters the capillary from above; an ORANGE pressure readout appears beside it as on-screen text. A glass rod comes down and pinches the capillary closed at one end. RED cells in the blocked segment stop flowing.
scenes.narration: A fine glass pipette slid into one capillary to record its pressure. Then he pressed the capillary shut with a fine glass rod.

scenes.tts: With the flow stopped, the trapped red cells drifted slowly. They moved toward the block when fluid was leaving through the wall. They moved away when fluid entered.
scenes.visual: Two stacked panels of the same blocked segment. Top: ORANGE arrows win, water leaves through the wall, RED cells drift toward the rod, label 'fluid leaving'. Bottom: BLUE arrows win, water enters, RED cells drift away from the rod, label 'fluid entering'.
scenes.narration: With the flow stopped, the trapped red cells drifted slowly. They moved toward the block when fluid was leaving through the wall. They moved away when fluid entered.

scenes.tts: From the cells' speed and the vessel's size, he worked out the fluid crossing each patch of wall. Then he plotted that rate against the pressure he had measured.
scenes.visual: A graph builds beside the vessel: x axis 'capillary pressure', y axis 'fluid crossing the wall (out is positive)'. Dots appear one at a time as the pipette readout changes. The zero line of the y axis is drawn in grey. Label 'schematic points'.
scenes.narration: From the cells' speed and the vessel's size, he worked out the fluid crossing each patch of wall. Then he plotted that rate against the pressure he had measured.

scenes.tts: If Starling was right, what should happen when capillary pressure falls below the pull of the plasma proteins? Which way should the fluid go?
scenes.visual: On the graph, a BLUE vertical marker labelled 'oncotic pull of frog plasma'. The region left of it is shaded and carries a question card. The dots to the left are hidden.
scenes.narration: If Starling was right, what should happen when capillary pressure falls below the pull of the plasma proteins? Which way should the fluid go?

scenes.visual: Predict pause. The question card holds; a 5-second ring timer counts down at bottom right.

scenes.tts: Fluid should come in, and it did. Filtration rose roughly in proportion to pressure. It fell to zero near the oncotic pressure of frog plasma, then reversed.
scenes.visual: The hidden dots appear below zero, left of the BLUE marker. A nearly straight line is drawn through all the points, crossing zero close to the marker, label 'filtration roughly proportional to pressure; zero near frog plasma oncotic pressure'. Line labelled 'schematic'.
scenes.narration: Fluid should come in, and it did. Filtration rose roughly in proportion to pressure. It fell to zero near the oncotic pressure of frog plasma, then reversed.

scenes.tts: So across the wall, the driving pressure is the push minus the pull. The more the push wins, the faster fluid leaves. When the pull wins, fluid comes in.
scenes.visual: The balance scale returns over the graph. On screen: 'net pressure = push − pull', and beneath it in small type '(P_c − P_i) − σ(π_c − π outside)', with a tiny note 'σ: the share of the protein pull that counts, since a few albumin cross'. As the ORANGE weight grows the dots climb the line; as it shrinks below the BLUE weight, arrows reverse and point inward.
scenes.narration: So across the wall, the driving pressure is the push minus the pull. The more the push wins, the faster fluid leaves. When the pull wins, fluid comes in.

scenes.tts: But Landis measured single capillaries in one frog tissue. His result ruled in the balance there. It did not show what every capillary does over hours.
scenes.visual: The frog mesentery shrinks into a small frame labelled 'one tissue, one species'. Beside it, a clock face labelled 'hours?' and outlines of other organs, each with a question mark.
scenes.narration: But Landis measured single capillaries in one frog tissue. His result ruled in the balance there. It did not show what every capillary does over hours.

scenes.tts: Later reviews concluded that a lasting return at the venous end lacks reproducible support. In most tissues, capillaries filter slowly, and lymph vessels carry the fluid back.
scenes.visual: One capillary from arterial end (left) to venous end (right). Small ORANGE outward arrows run along its whole length; the expected big inward BLUE arrows at the venous end fade out, stamped 'not supported as a general account'. A blind-ended GREEN lymph vessel beside it collects the seeping fluid and carries it away toward a vein.
scenes.narration: Later reviews concluded that a lasting return at the venous end lacks reproducible support. In most tissues, capillaries filter slowly, and lymph vessels carry the fluid back.

scenes.visual: Hex card. Line: 'Push minus pull decides which way fluid crosses the wall.'
